claim: Caenorhabditis elegans halts postembryonic growth and development shortly after hatching in response to monomethyl branched-chain fatty acid (mmBCFA) deficiency.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans halts postembryonic growth and development shortly after hatching in response to monomethyl branched-chain fatty acid (mmBCFA) deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript and is a foundational observation for the current study.

claim: An mmBCFA-derived sphingolipid, d17iso-glucosylceramide, is a critical metabolite in regulating growth and development.
source: Here, we report that an mmBCFA-derived sphingolipid, d17iso-glucosylceramide, is a critical metabolite in regulating growth and development.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and biochemical experiments described in the manuscript showing that d17iso-GlcCer mediates the essential role of mmBCFAs.

claim: The d17iso-glucosylceramide lipid function is mediated by TORC1 and antagonized by the NPRL-2/3 complex in the intestine.
source: Further analysis indicated that this lipid function is mediated by TORC1 and antagonized by the NPRL-2/3 complex in the intestine.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic suppression experiments and RNAi studies showing that TORC1 acts downstream of d17iso-GlcCer and is negatively regulated by NPRL-2/3.

claim: The essential lipid function is bypassed by activating TORC1 or inhibiting NPRL-2/3.
source: Strikingly, the essential lipid function is bypassed by activating TORC1 or inhibiting NPRL-2/3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that constitutive activation of TORC1 or loss of NPRL-2/3 function allows mmBCFA-deficient animals to develop normally.

claim: The target of rapamycin (TOR) complexes (TORC1 and TORC2) function in sensing various nutrient signals.
source: The target of rapamycin (TOR) complexes (TORC1 and TORC2) are known to function in sensing various nutrient signals (Ma and Blenis, 2009; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012; Zoncu et al., 2012), and their roles are connected to growth, metabolism, stress responses, and cancers (Hansen et al., 2008; He and Klionsky, 2009; Howell and Manning, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on TOR complexes.

claim: Roles of lipid molecules as signals to TOR complexes in controlling postembryonic growth and development were not known prior to this study.
source: While amino acids, energy, and growth factors have been described as nutrient inputs to TOR complexes, roles of lipid molecules as signals to these systems in controlling postembryonic growth and development were not known.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior knowledge in the literature.

claim: When hatched in food-free surroundings, C. elegans enters a quiescent state termed L1 diapause.
source: When hatched in food-free surroundings, this nematode enters a quiescent state, termed L1 diapause (Johnson et al., 1984; Munoz and Riddle, 2003; Baugh and Sternberg, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on L1 diapause.

claim: An insulin/IGF-1 receptor signaling (IIS) pathway plays a critical role in the induction of L1 diapause and survival of developmentally arrested animals.
source: An insulin/IGF-1 receptor signaling (IIS) pathway plays a critical role in the induction of L1 diapause and survival of the developmentally arrested animals (Gems et al., 1998; Baugh and Sternberg, 2006; Kniazeva et al., 2008; Lee and Ashrafi, 2008; Jones et al., 2009; Soukas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the IIS pathway.

claim: TOR complexes play prominent roles in regulating postembryonic growth and lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, TOR complexes have also been indicated to play prominent roles in regulating postembryonic growth and lifespan in C. elegans (Vellai et al., 2003; Syntichaki et al., 2007; Hansen et al., 2008; Honjoh et al., 2009; Lucanic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on TOR complexes in C. elegans.

claim: Monomethyl branched-chain fatty acids (mmBCFAs) are widely present in bacteria, plants, and animals, including humans.
source: Monomethyl branched-chain fatty acids (mmBCFAs) are widely present in bacteria, plants, and animals, including humans (Nicolaides and Ray, 1965; Ran-Ressler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the distribution of mmBCFAs.

claim: In mammals, mmBCFAs are derived from branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs).
source: In mammals, mmBCFAs are derived from branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) (Morii and Kaneda, 1982; Oku et al., 1994), although the remainder of the de novo pathway has not been delineated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on mmBCFA biosynthesis in mammals.

claim: The physiological roles of mmBCFAs are essentially unknown.
source: The physiological roles of these FA variants are essentially unknown, even though they were found to be present at very high levels in certain tissues (Nicolaides and Ray, 1965; Ran-Ressler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior knowledge in the literature despite the presence of mmBCFAs in tissues.

claim: In C. elegans, readily detectable mmBCFAs C15ISO and C17ISO are synthesized from the BCAA leucine.
source: In C. elegans, readily detectable mmBCFAs C15ISO and C17ISO are synthesized from the BCAA leucine (Kniazeva et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on mmBCFA biosynthesis in C. elegans.

claim: The key enzymes in mmBCFA de novo synthesis pathway, including the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDC), an FA elongase (ELO-5), and an acyl CoA synthetase (ACS-1), are evolutionarily conserved.
source: The key enzymes in this de novo synthesis pathway, including the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDC), an FA elongase (ELO-5), and an acyl CoA synthetase (ACS-1), are evolutionarily conserved (Kniazeva et al., 2004, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the enzymes involved in mmBCFA biosynthesis.

claim: Newly hatched C. elegans that are deficient for mmBCFAs cannot initiate postembryonic growth and development, and instead enter L1 diapause.
source: We have previously shown that newly hatched C. elegans that are deficient for mmBCFAs cannot initiate postembryonic growth and development, and instead enter L1 diapause.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies by the authors.

claim: The developmental arrest caused by mmBCFA deficiency is independent of the IIS pathway.
source: Further genetic analysis suggested that this developmental arrest is independent of the IIS pathway (Kniazeva et al., 2004, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: elo-5 loss-of-function mutants are deficient for mmBCFAs and are developmentally arrested at the early L1 stage.
source: elo-5 loss-of-function mutants (termed elo-5(−) hereafter) are deficient for mmBCFAs and are developmentally arrested at the early L1 stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies and is a foundational observation for the current study.

claim: The elo-5(−) phenotype is completely rescued by dietary supplementation of mmBCFAs.
source: This phenotype is completely rescued by dietary supplementation of mmBCFAs (Kniazeva et al., 2004, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mmBCFA-deficient elo-5(−) larvae, the amount of mmBCFA-containing sphingolipids were dramatically reduced.
source: We found that in mmBCFA-deficient elo-5(−) larvae, the amount of mmBCFA-containing sphingolipids were dramatically reduced and thus asked if this mmBCFA function is mediated by a sphingolipid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the current study.

claim: Sphingolipids are a class of well-known bioactive lipids.
source: Sphingolipids are a class of well-known bioactive lipids (Hannun and Obeid, 2008) that are composed of an aliphatic amino alcohol backbone called the sphingoid base or long chain base (LCB), and usually an N-acylated fatty acid (FA) side chain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In C. elegans, both the LCB and the FA side chain may derive from mmBCFAs, such as C15ISO and C17ISO.
source: In C. elegans, both the LCB and the FA side chain may derive from mmBCFAs, such as C15ISO and C17ISO (Chitwood et al., 1995; Gerdt et al., 1997; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: d17iso-sphinganine (d17iso-SPA) was purified from the bacteria S. spiritivorum.
source: Because the d17iso-LCB was not commercially available, we purified d17iso-sphinganine (d17iso-SPA; Figure 1A) from a d17iso-sphingolipid producing bacteria S. spiritivorum (Yabuuchi et al., 1983) using mass spectrometry analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the manuscript and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Purified d17iso-SPA, but not a chemically synthesized c17iso-sphingolipid with a straight-chain d18:1-LCB or a straight-chain LCB d16-SPA, was sufficient to overcome elo-5(−) L1 arrest.
source: This purified d17iso-SPA fraction, but not a chemically synthesized c17iso-sphingolipid with a straight-chain d18:1-LCB or a straight-chain LCB d16-SPA, was found to be sufficient to overcome elo-5(−) L1 arrest (Figure 1B,C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Efficient rescue of elo-5(−) was achieved with a custom synthesized d17iso-SPA.
source: Additionally, efficient rescue was also achieved with a custom synthesized d17iso-SPA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: d17iso-sphingolipid is sufficient to promote the postembryonic growth and development of mmBCFA-deficient animals.
source: Therefore, d17iso-sphingolipid is sufficient to promote the postembryonic growth and development of mmBCFA-deficient animals.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with d17iso-SPA.

claim: d17iso-SPA suppressed the L1 arrest at a much lower concentration than C15ISO or C17ISO.
source: First, we fed elo-5(−) larvae with various quantities of C15ISO, C17ISO, or d17iso-SPA. We observed that d17iso-SPA suppressed the L1 arrest at a much lower concentration than C15ISO or C17ISO (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Low concentrations of d17iso-SPA suppressed the L1 arrest without restoring mmBCFA levels.
source: Second, we observed that the low concentrations of d17iso-SPA suppressed the L1 arrest without restoring mmBCFA levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Supplementation with d17iso-SPA, but not mmBCFAs, suppressed the L1 arrest phenotype caused by feeding RNAi of sptl-1.
source: Finally, we found that supplementation with d17iso-SPA, but not mmBCFAs, also suppressed the L1 arrest phenotype caused by feeding RNAi of sptl-1, a gene encoding a serine palmitoyltransferase homolog in C. elegans required for d17iso-SPA biosynthesis (Figure 1A,B; Seamen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: mmBCFAs promote postembryonic development through d17iso-SPA.
source: We thus conclude that mmBCFAs promote postembryonic development through d17iso-SPA.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing that d17iso-SPA rescues mmBCFA deficiency.

claim: fath-1(C25A1.5) encodes a homolog of mammalian fatty acid 2-hydrolase (FA2H) responsible for the synthesis of the FA side chain of ceramides.
source: Specifically, fath-1(C25A1.5) encodes a homolog of mammalian fatty acid 2-hydrolase (FA2H) responsible for the synthesis of the FA side chain of ceramides, whereas cgt-1 and cgt-3 encode two ceramide glucosyltransferases that glucosylate ceramides to GlcCer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of gene function and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: cgt-1 and cgt-3 encode two ceramide glucosyltransferases that glucosylate ceramides to GlcCer.
source: Specifically, fath-1(C25A1.5) encodes a homolog of mammalian fatty acid 2-hydrolase (FA2H) responsible for the synthesis of the FA side chain of ceramides, whereas cgt-1 and cgt-3 encode two ceramide glucosyltransferases that glucosylate ceramides to GlcCer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of gene function and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Both fath-1(RNAi)-treated animals and the cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) double mutant cause larval arrest.
source: Both fath-1(RNAi)-treated animals (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1) and the cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) double mutant (Marza et al., 2009) cause larval arrest.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The arrest caused by fath-1(RNAi) or cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) could not be overcome by feeding d17iso-SPA.
source: We found the arrest under either condition could not be overcome by feeding d17iso-SPA (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Disrupting the function of glycosyltransferases that further modify GlcCer does not cause larval arrest.
source: Disrupting the function of glycosyltransferases that further modify GlcCer does not cause larval arrest (Griffitts et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: d17iso-glucosylceramide (d17iso-GlcCer) may be the lipid molecule that mediates the role of mmBCFAs and d17iso-SPA in promoting postembryonic growth and development in C. elegans.
source: These results suggest that d17iso-glucosylceramide (d17iso-GlcCer) (Figure 1A) may be the lipid molecule that mediates the role of mmBCFAs and d17iso-SPA in promoting postembryonic growth and development in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments showing that enzymes downstream of d17iso-SPA are required for rescue.

claim: ku540 was the only mutation that rescued elo-5(−) larvae to adults and permitted growth for more than one generation without mmBCFA supplementation or restoration of mmBCFA synthesis.
source: Among four suppressors identified in this screen, and the tat-2 mutations from a previous elo-5(−) suppressor screen (Seamen et al., 2009), ku540 was the only mutation that rescued elo-5(−) larvae to adults and permitted growth for more than one generation without mmBCFA supplementation or restoration of mmBCFA synthesis (Figure 2B–E; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: elo-5(−);ku540 homozygous animals could propagate continuously, even though they displayed slow growth, smaller body size, and smaller brood size.
source: In fact, elo-5(−);ku540 homozygous animals could propagate continuously, even though they displayed slow growth, smaller body size, and smaller brood size (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: elo-5(−);ku540 animals had no detectable C15ISO-containing or C17ISO-containing lipids.
source: elo-5(−);ku540 animals had no detectable C15ISO-containing or C17ISO-containing lipids (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry and gas chromatography data shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and supplementary figures.

claim: In contrast to wild type animals, elo-5(-);ku540 animals had ceramides and glucosylceramides containing straight chain d16LCB rather than d17isoLCB.
source: In contrast to wild type animals, elo-5(-);ku540 animals had ceramides and glucosylceramides containing straight chain d16LCB rather than d17isoLCB (Figure 2F,G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), which is similar to the elo-5(−) single mutant (Entchev et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2F, 2G, and supplementary figures, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The suppression of L1 arrest by the ku540 mutation is neither due to a change in mmBCFA nor the metabolism of the derived sphingolipids.
source: These data indicated that the suppression of L1 arrest by the ku540 mutation is neither due to a change in mmBCFA nor the metabolism of the derived sphingolipids.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the mass spectrometry and gas chromatography data.

claim: ku540 renders mmBCFAs nonessential for C. elegans development.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that ku540 renders mmBCFAs nonessential for C. elegans development.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that ku540 suppresses mmBCFA deficiency without restoring mmBCFA levels.

claim: The L1 arrest caused by RNAi of fath-1, or mutating both cgt-1 and cgt-3, was effectively suppressed by ku540.
source: We found that the L1 arrest under both conditions, just like the arrest caused by elo-5(−), was effectively suppressed by ku540 (Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H, 2I, and supplementary figures.

claim: d17iso-GlcCer mediated the roles of mmBCFAs and d17iso-SPA in postembryonic development.
source: These results provided strong evidence that d17iso-GlcCer mediated the roles of mmBCFAs and d17iso-SPA in postembryonic development.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic suppression experiments.

claim: ku540 bypasses the requirement of mmBCFAs and d17iso-GlcCer in development by modifying a regulatory function downstream of d17iso-GlcCer.
source: Taken together, our biochemical and genetic data indicate that ku540 bypasses the requirement of mmBCFAs and d17iso-GlcCer in development and does so by modifying a regulatory function downstream of d17iso-GlcCer.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical and genetic data.

claim: The gene containing the ku540 mutation was cloned by genetic mapping and whole-genome sequencing.
source: We cloned the gene containing the ku540 mutation by genetic mapping and whole-genome sequencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The gene was annotated as F35H10.7 (wormbase.org) that encodes a protein structurally conserved from budding yeast (NPR3, Nitrogen Permease Regulator 3) to humans (NPRL-3, Nitrogen Permease Regulator Like 3).
source: The gene was annotated as F35H10.7 (wormbase.org) that encodes a protein structurally conserved from budding yeast (NPR3, Nitrogen Permease Regulator 3) to humans (NPRL-3, Nitrogen Permease Regulator Like 3; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: nprl-3(ku540) is a C-T substitution that changes a conserved proline to serine.
source: nprl-3(ku540) is a C-T substitution that changes a conserved proline to serine (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RNAi of nprl-3 by dsRNA injection rescued the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) and cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) animals.
source: RNAi of nprl-3 by dsRNA injection also rescued the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) and cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) animals (Figure 3C), indicating that ku540 is likely a partial loss-of-function or reduction-of-function mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ku540 is likely a partial loss-of-function or reduction-of-function mutation.
source: RNAi of nprl-3 by dsRNA injection also rescued the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) and cgt-1(−);cgt-3(−) animals (Figure 3C), indicating that ku540 is likely a partial loss-of-function or reduction-of-function mutation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RNAi of nprl-3 mimics the ku540 phenotype.

claim: A transcriptional GFP fusion transgene (nprl-3::GFP) was observed to express ubiquitously throughout development and adulthood.
source: A transcriptional GFP fusion transgene (nprl-3::GFP) was observed to express ubiquitously throughout development and adulthood (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NPR3 was shown to form a heterodimer with NPR2.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NPR3 was shown to form a heterodimer with NPR2. Mutations in both proteins cause multiple growth defects when cells were cultured in low-quality amino acid conditions (Neklesa and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: Mutations in NPR2 and NPR3 in yeast cause multiple growth defects when cells were cultured in low-quality amino acid conditions.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NPR3 was shown to form a heterodimer with NPR2. Mutations in both proteins cause multiple growth defects when cells were cultured in low-quality amino acid conditions (Neklesa and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: RNAi by dsRNA injection of the C. elegans NPR2 homolog nprl-2 (F49E8.1) suppressed the developmental arrest of elo-5(−) larvae.
source: We found that RNAi by dsRNA injection of the C. elegans NPR2 homolog nprl-2 (F49E8.1) also suppressed the developmental arrest of elo-5(−) larvae (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NPRL-2 and NPRL-3 in C. elegans may function in a complex to negatively impact mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer-mediated L1 growth.
source: This suggested that NPRL-2 and NPRL-3 in C. elegans may also function in a complex to negatively impact mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer-mediated L1 growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RNAi of nprl-2 mimics the effect of nprl-3(ku540).

claim: The NPR2/3 complex was proposed to be a negative regulator of the TOR pathway in S. cerevisiae.
source: The NPR2/3 complex was proposed to be a negative regulator of the TOR pathway in S. cerevisiae, based on the observations that mutations in these two genes caused growth defects in an amino acid scarce environment and that the defects could be effectively suppressed by blocking the TOR pathway (Neklesa and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: Reducing, but not eliminating, TORC1 activity may reverse the rescue effects of nprl-3(ku540) on elo-5(−) mutant background.
source: We reasoned that if reducing nprl-2/3 activity rescued elo-5(−) L1 growth by up-regulating the TORC1 pathway in C. elegans, then reducing, but not eliminating, TORC1 activity may reverse the rescue effects of nprl-3(ku540) on elo-5(−) mutant background.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the proposed relationship between NPRL-2/3 and TORC1.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans has orthologs of key components of mammalian TORC1, including regulatory elements raga-1 (RagA) and rheb-1 (Rheb).
source: Caenorhabditis elegans has orthologs of key components of mammalian TORC1, including regulatory elements raga-1 (RagA) and rheb-1 (Rheb) (Long et al., 2002; Schreiber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Feeding RNAi of raga-1 and rheb-1 have been shown to be specific and effective to reduce, but not eliminate, TORC1 function.
source: Feeding RNAi of raga-1 and rheb-1 have been shown to be specific and effective to reduce, but not eliminate, TORC1 function (Hansen et al., 2007; Syntichaki et al., 2007; Lemire et al., 2009; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: While nprl-3(ku540) effectively suppressed the L1 arrest phenotype of elo-5(−), the suppression dramatically decreased when raga-1(RNAi) or rheb-1(RNAi) were applied to the elo-5(−) nprl-3(ku540) double mutant.
source: While nprl-3(ku540) effectively suppressed the L1 arrest phenotype of elo-5(−), the suppression dramatically decreased when raga-1(RNAi) or rheb-1(RNAi) were applied to the elo-5(−) nprl-3(ku540) double mutant (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The rescue effect of nprl-3(ku540) on elo-5(−) depends on intact TORC1 activity.
source: This indicates that the rescue effect of nprl-3(ku540) on elo-5(−) depends on intact TORC1 activity.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing that reducing TORC1 activity reverses the suppression by nprl-3(ku540).

claim: The effects of raga-1(RNAi) and rheb-1(RNAi) were essentially eliminated by C17ISO supplementation.
source: We found that the effects of raga-1(RNAi) and rheb-1(RNAi) in the above tests were essentially eliminated by C17ISO supplementation (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The reversal of the nprl-3(ku540) suppression by raga-1(RNAi) or rheb-1(RNAi) depends on mmBCFA deficiency.
source: This result further indicates that the reversal of the nprl-3(ku540) suppression by raga-1(RNAi) or rheb-1(RNAi) depends on mmBCFA deficiency.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that C17ISO supplementation eliminates the effects of raga-1(RNAi) and rheb-1(RNAi).

claim: Reducing, but not eliminating, TORC1 activity neutralized the effect of nprl-3(ku540) and restored the L1 arrest phenotype of elo-5(−).
source: In other words, reducing, but not eliminating, TORC1 activity neutralized the effect of nprl-3(ku540) and restored the L1 arrest phenotype of elo-5(−).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments.

claim: elo-5(−) nprl-3(ku540) animals treated with ife-2(RNAi) or rsks-1(RNAi), with or without C17ISO supplement, yielded results similar to those obtained with raga-1(RNAi) and rheb-1(RNAi).
source: We found that elo-5(−) nprl-3(ku540) animals treated with ife-2(RNAi) or rsks-1(RNAi), with or without C17ISO supplement, yielded results similar to those obtained with raga-1(RNAi) and rheb-1(RNAi) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: TORC1 acts downstream of d17iso-GlcCer and is negatively regulated by NPRL-3.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that TORC1 acts downstream of d17iso-GlcCer and is negatively regulated by NPRL-3.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and RNAi experiments.

claim: The let-363/TOR(−) mutations cause late larval arrest and other severe defects.
source: The let-363/TOR(−) mutations cause late larval arrest and other severe defects (Long et al., 2002), but injection RNAi causes an early embryonic lethal phenotype (Sonnichsen et al., 2005), indicating that LET-363/TOR, a key component of both TORC1 and TORC2, plays critical regulatory roles in a broad range of developmental stages and a maternal effect largely masks its roles in earlier stages, including its likely functions during L1 growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LET-363/TOR, a key component of both TORC1 and TORC2, plays critical regulatory roles in a broad range of developmental stages.
source: The let-363/TOR(−) mutations cause late larval arrest and other severe defects (Long et al., 2002), but injection RNAi causes an early embryonic lethal phenotype (Sonnichsen et al., 2005), indicating that LET-363/TOR, a key component of both TORC1 and TORC2, plays critical regulatory roles in a broad range of developmental stages and a maternal effect largely masks its roles in earlier stages, including its likely functions during L1 growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the different phenotypes caused by mutations and RNAi of let-363/TOR.

claim: A maternal effect largely masks the roles of LET-363/TOR in earlier stages, including its likely functions during L1 growth.
source: The let-363/TOR(−) mutations cause late larval arrest and other severe defects (Long et al., 2002), but injection RNAi causes an early embryonic lethal phenotype (Sonnichsen et al., 2005), indicating that LET-363/TOR, a key component of both TORC1 and TORC2, plays critical regulatory roles in a broad range of developmental stages and a maternal effect largely masks its roles in earlier stages, including its likely functions during L1 growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the different phenotypes caused by mutations and RNAi of let-363/TOR.

claim: The defects caused by feeding RNAi of let-363/TOR are more severe than that by feeding RNAi of other TORC1 components.
source: The defects caused by feeding RNAi of let-363/TOR (Long et al., 2002) are more severe than that by feeding RNAi of other TORC1 components, described above.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the current study and a citation to a previous study.

claim: elo-5(−) nprl-3(−);let-363(RNAi) animals displayed pleiotropic phenotypes that could not be rescued by C17ISO supplement.
source: elo-5(−) nprl-3(−);let-363(RNAi) animals displayed pleiotropic phenotypes that could not be rescued by C17ISO supplement (Table 1), which is consistent with TORC1 acting downstream of ELO-5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The pleiotropic phenotypes of elo-5(−) nprl-3(−);let-363(RNAi) animals are consistent with TORC1 acting downstream of ELO-5.
source: elo-5(−) nprl-3(−);let-363(RNAi) animals displayed pleiotropic phenotypes that could not be rescued by C17ISO supplement (Table 1), which is consistent with TORC1 acting downstream of ELO-5.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that C17ISO cannot rescue the phenotypes.

claim: Constitutive activation of TORC1 should be sufficient to overcome the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) animals, mimicking the effect of nprl-3(ku540).
source: If d17iso-GlcCer mainly acts through TORC1 for the growth regulation function, constitutive activation of TORC1 should be sufficient to overcome the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) animals, mimicking the effect of nprl-3(ku540).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the proposed relationship between d17iso-GlcCer and TORC1.

claim: Fusion of Raptor with a C-terminal lysosome localization signal from Rap-1 can localize mTOR to the lysosome and thus constitutively activate the TOR pathway.
source: We first followed the scheme by Sancak et al. (2010), in which fusion of one of the TOR binding partners, Raptor, with a C-terminal lysosome localization signal from Rap-1 can localize mTOR to the lysosome and thus constitutively activate the TOR pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both Rap-1 and Raptor proteins are highly conserved in C. elegans (encoded by rap-1 and daf-15).
source: Both Rap-1 and Raptor proteins are highly conserved in C. elegans (encoded by rap-1 and daf-15; Long et al., 2002; Pellis-van Berkel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 56.0% of elo-5(−) mutants carrying daf-15::rap-1(22) bypassed L1 arrest and reached L3 to adult stage.
source: We found that 56.0% of elo-5(−) mutants carrying daf-15::rap-1(22) bypassed L1 arrest and reached L3 to adult stage (n = 161; normalized against elo-5(−/+) heterozygotes containing the transgene; Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Hyperactivation of TORC1 was sufficient to support L1 growth in mmBCFA-depleted animals.
source: This indicates that hyperactivation of TORC1 was sufficient to support L1 growth in mmBCFA-depleted animals.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with daf-15::rap-1(22).

claim: 50.4% of elo-5(−) mutants containing the raga-1Q63L transgene bypassed L1 arrest and reached L3–L4 stage.
source: We found that 50.4% of elo-5(−) mutants containing the raga-1Q63L transgene bypassed L1 arrest and reached L3–L4 stage (n = 248, p=1.0 × 10−6; normalized against elo-5(−/+) heterozygotes containing the transgene; Figure 4A) while none of elo-5(−) mutants without this transgene did (n = 136).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: raga-1Q63L has been proven to constitutively activate TORC1 both in mammals and C. elegans.
source: The second TORC1-activating transgene used was raga-1Q63L that has been proven to constitutively activate TORC1 both in mammals and C. elegans (Kim et al., 2008; Schreiber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 41.4% of elo-5(−) animals carrying the rheb-1Q71LQ72D transgene grew beyond the L1 stage.
source: Finally, we also tested a third TORC1-activating transgene, rheb-1Q71LQ72D, and found that it also permitted 41.4% of elo-5(−) animals to grow beyond the L1 stage (n = 169; normalized against elo-5(−/+) heterozygotes containing the transgene; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TORC1 acts downstream of d17iso-GlcCer to promote L1 growth and development and this activity is negatively regulated by NPRL-2/3.
source: These results led to the conclusion that TORC1 acts downstream of d17iso-GlcCer to promote L1 growth and development and that this activity is negatively regulated by NPRL-2/3.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing that constitutive activation of TORC1 bypasses mmBCFA deficiency.

claim: Previous studies on elo-5, acs-1, tat-2, and cgt-1/cgt-3 mutants suggested that biosynthesis and localization of mmBCFAs and their derived sphingolipids in the intestine are essential and sufficient for postembryonic development.
source: Previous studies on elo-5, acs-1, tat-2, and cgt-1/cgt-3 mutants suggested that biosynthesis and localization of mmBCFAs and their derived sphingolipids in the intestine are essential and sufficient for postembryonic development (Marza et al., 2009; Seamen et al., 2009; Kniazeva et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The fact that elo-5(−);nprl-3(ku540) animals treated with ife-2 RNAi, that targets intestinal but not neuronal expression of the gene, are L1 arrested points to the requirement of TORC1 activity in the intestine.
source: The fact that elo-5(−);nprl-3(ku540) animals treated with ife-2 RNAi, that targets intestinal but not neuronal expression of the gene (Syntichaki et al., 2007), are L1 arrested (Table 1) also points to the requirement of TORC1 activity in the intestine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and a citation to a previous study.

claim: elo-5(−) animals containing an intestinal-specific ges-1 promoter-driven raga-1Q63L transgene bypassed the L1 arrest (37.9%, n = 132).
source: We found that elo-5(−) animals containing this transgene bypassed the L1 arrest (37.9%, n = 132, normalized against elo-5(−/+) heterozygotes containing the transgene; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rescue with the intestinal expression of raga-1Q63L was similar to that by a ubiquitously expressed raga-1Q63L transgene.
source: The rescue with the intestinal expression was similar to that by a ubiquitously expressed raga-1Q63L transgene (above).
evidence: This claim is a comparison of experimental results.

claim: A neuronal-specific rgef-1 promoter–driven raga-1Q63L could not suppress the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) animals (0%, n > 100).
source: A neuronal-specific rgef-1 promoter–driven (Brignull et al., 2006) raga-1Q63L, however, could not suppress the L1 arrest of elo-5(−) animals (0%, n > 100).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The intestinal d17iso-GlcCer/TORC1 pathway regulates postembryonic growth.
source: These results suggest that the intestinal d17iso-GlcCer/TORC1 pathway regulates postembryonic growth.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Localization of FIB-1, a Box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) was used as a marker of TORC1 activation in C. elegans.
source: Because the biochemical assay for p70S6K phosphorylation has not been established in C. elegans' TOR-related studies, we adopted the strategy by Sheaffer et al. (2008), where localization of FIB-1, a Box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) was used as a marker of TORC1 activation in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In wild-type animals, FIB-1 is highly expressed and localized in the nucleolus, where it methylates pre-rRNAs during ribosome maturation.
source: In wild-type animals, FIB-1 is highly expressed and localized in the nucleolus, where it methylates pre-rRNAs during ribosome maturation, but the expression is decreased and no longer localized to the nucleolus in let-363/TOR(−) animals (Sheaffer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of FIB-1 is decreased and no longer localized to the nucleolus in let-363/TOR(−) animals.
source: In wild-type animals, FIB-1 is highly expressed and localized in the nucleolus, where it methylates pre-rRNAs during ribosome maturation, but the expression is decreased and no longer localized to the nucleolus in let-363/TOR(−) animals (Sheaffer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The nucleolar localized FIB-1 was dramatically reduced in intestinal cells of mmBCFA-deficient [elo-5(RNAi)] animals.
source: We found that the nucleolar localized FIB-1 was dramatically reduced in intestinal cells of mmBCFA-deficient [elo-5(RNAi)] animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: nprl-3(−) rescued the FIB-1 expression and nucleolar localization in elo-5(−) back to that of wild type.
source: Furthermore, nprl-3(−) rescued the FIB-1 expression and nucleolar localization in elo-5(−) back to that of wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TORC1 is the key downstream factor mediating mmBCFA and d17iso-GlcCer functions in the intestine to promote postembryonic growth and development.
source: Combining the results from the functional and biochemical assays described above, we conclude that TORC1 is the key downstream factor mediating mmBCFA and d17iso-GlcCer functions in the intestine to promote postembryonic growth and development (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the functional and biochemical assays, and is illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: This discovery reveals a specific link between lipids and the TORC1 signaling pathway.
source: This discovery reveals a specific link between lipids and the TORC1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Both ceramide and TORC1 have been individually implicated for roles in stress response, apoptosis, cancers, and other cellular processes by studies in C. elegans and mammals.
source: Both ceramide and TORC1 have been individually implicated for roles in stress response, apoptosis, cancers, and other cellular processes by studies in C. elegans and mammals (Hannun and Obeid, 2008; Hansen et al., 2008; He and Klionsky, 2009; Howell and Manning, 2011; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012; Menuz et al., 2009; Zoncu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some of the functions of ceramide and TORC1 may be mediated by the GlcCer/TORC1 signaling pathway.
source: It is conceivable that some of these functions are mediated by this GlcCer/TORC1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The GlcCer/TORC1 pathway may serve as a 'check point' to coordinate metabolic status in the intestine with postembryonic growth and development.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that this GlcCer/TORC1 pathway may serve as a 'check point' to coordinate metabolic status in the intestine with postembryonic growth and development.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: d17iso-GlcCer is a sphingolipid metabolite rather than a nutrient directly absorbed from food.
source: d17iso-GlcCer is a sphingolipid metabolite rather than a nutrient directly absorbed from food (Merrill et al., 1997); it is the product of a long biosynthetic pathway involving many enzymatic steps and thus may reflect the availability of many metabolites and enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: d17iso-GlcCer is the product of a long biosynthetic pathway involving many enzymatic steps and thus may reflect the availability of many metabolites and enzymes.
source: d17iso-GlcCer is a sphingolipid metabolite rather than a nutrient directly absorbed from food (Merrill et al., 1997); it is the product of a long biosynthetic pathway involving many enzymatic steps and thus may reflect the availability of many metabolites and enzymes.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the nature of the biosynthetic pathway.

claim: The long lipid synthesis pathway is unlikely part of a mechanism to specifically sense the level of essential amino acids.
source: Although leucine is a precursor molecule of mmBCFA biosynthesis, this long lipid synthesis pathway is unlikely part of a mechanism to specifically sense the level of essential amino acids.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the complexity of the pathway.

claim: mmBCFA levels are stable in starved L1 larvae.
source: Furthermore, mmBCFA levels are stable in starved L1 larvae (Kniazeva et al., 2008; Figure 4—figure supplement 4C), suggesting that mmBCFA levels do not directly reflect the feeding status through a direct substrate–product relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: mmBCFA levels do not directly reflect the feeding status through a direct substrate–product relationship.
source: Furthermore, mmBCFA levels are stable in starved L1 larvae (Kniazeva et al., 2008; Figure 4—figure supplement 4C), suggesting that mmBCFA levels do not directly reflect the feeding status through a direct substrate–product relationship.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mmBCFA levels are stable in starved larvae.

claim: There are several reported leucine-sensing mechanisms, based on studies using tissue culture cells.
source: There are several reported leucine-sensing mechanisms, based on studies using tissue culture cells (Bonfils et al., 2012; Duran et al., 2012; Han et al., 2012; Zoncu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Supplementing elo-5(−) animals with a high level of dietary leucine (10 mM) did not suppress the L1 arrest phenotype.
source: To test if such a pathway acts in parallel to the mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer pathway to promote TORC1 in the C. elegans intestine, we supplemented elo-5(−) animals with a high level of dietary leucine (10 mM) and failed to observe any suppression of the L1 arrest phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with the idea that TORC1 activation by mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer is essential in the intestine of L1 larvae and cannot be effectively compensated by another leucine/TORC1 mechanism in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: TORC1 activation by mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer is essential in the intestine of L1 larvae and cannot be effectively compensated by another leucine/TORC1 mechanism in C. elegans.
source: To test if such a pathway acts in parallel to the mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer pathway to promote TORC1 in the C. elegans intestine, we supplemented elo-5(−) animals with a high level of dietary leucine (10 mM) and failed to observe any suppression of the L1 arrest phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with the idea that TORC1 activation by mmBCFA/d17iso-GlcCer is essential in the intestine of L1 larvae and cannot be effectively compensated by another leucine/TORC1 mechanism in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the leucine supplementation experiment.

claim: Both the IIS and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways play critical roles in the regulation of postembryonic growth and development in response to nutrient/food availability in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, both the IIS and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways have been shown to play critical roles in the regulation of postembryonic growth and development in response to nutrient/food availability (Baugh and Sternberg, 2006; Mukhopadhyay and Tissenbaum, 2007; Fielenbach and Antebi, 2008; Lee and Ashrafi, 2008; Jones et al., 2009; Soukas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GlcCer/TORC1 pathway is initiated in the intestine and is independent of the IIS pathway.
source: Our previous data and this study indicated that the GlcCer/TORC1 pathway is initiated in the intestine (Figure 4) and is independent of the IIS pathway (Kniazeva et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the current study and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The GlcCer/TORC1 pathway is DAF-7/TGF-β pathway independent.
source: Our additional analysis also suggests that the GlcCer/TORC1 pathway is DAF-7/TGF-β pathway independent (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The independence of the GlcCer/TORC1 pathway from IIS and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways may facilitate its role to promote specific developmental events under specific physiological conditions.
source: This independence may facilitate the role of such a pathway to promote specific developmental events under specific physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the independence of the pathway.

claim: The components of TORC1 are conserved between C. elegans and mammals.
source: There are several reasons for us to believe that such a GlcCer/TORC1 pathway is likely conserved in mammals. First, the components of TORC1 are conserved between C. elegans and mammals.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of protein conservation.

claim: The NPRL-3 protein is conserved in all eukaryotes, and its negative regulatory role on TOR has been characterized in budding yeast.
source: The NPRL-3 protein we identified in this pathway is conserved in all eukaryotes, and its negative regulatory role on TOR has been characterized in budding yeast (Neklesa and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Several proteins (such as NPR2 and IML1) that are reported to form a complex with NPR3 in budding yeast have orthologs in C. elegans as well as mammals.
source: Several proteins (such as NPR2 and IML1) that are reported to form a complex with NPR3 in budding yeast have orthologs in C. elegans as well as mammals (Neklesa and Davis, 2009; Wu and Tu, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPRL2 (human ortholog of NPR2) and DEPDC5 (human ortholog of IML1) have been reported to function as tumor suppressors.
source: NPRL2 (human ortholog of NPR2) and DEPDC5 (human ortholog of IML1) have been reported to function as tumor suppressors (Merrill et al., 1997; Li et al., 2004; Neklesa and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tumor suppressor property of NPRL2 and DEPDC5 is consistent with the role of this complex in repressing TOR-mediated growth regulation that was identified in budding yeast and this study.
source: This property is consistent with the role of this complex in repressing TOR-mediated growth regulation that was identified in budding yeast and this study.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the known functions of these proteins.

claim: A role for GlcCer in nutrient sensing is consistent with studies showing that ceramide and sphingolipids play roles in cell signaling and growth control in both invertebrates and mammals.
source: Second, a role for GlcCer in nutrient sensing is consistent with studies showing that ceramide and sphingolipids play roles in cell signaling and growth control in both invertebrates and mammals (Deng et al., 2008; Hannun and Obeid, 2008; Menuz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mouse mutants with blocked GlcCer biosynthesis die as early embryos, suggesting the essential role of these lipids in growth and development.
source: The finding that mouse mutants with blocked GlcCer biosynthesis die as early embryos suggests the essential role of these lipids in growth and development (Yamashita et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The TOR pathway is down-regulated by inhibiting the abnormally high GlcCer biosynthesis in polycystic kidney disease in mouse models.
source: Third, the TOR pathway is down-regulated by inhibiting the abnormally high GlcCer biosynthesis in polycystic kidney disease in mouse models (Natoli et al., 2010), suggesting a possible conserved link between GlcCer and TOR activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a possible conserved link between GlcCer and TOR activities.
source: Third, the TOR pathway is down-regulated by inhibiting the abnormally high GlcCer biosynthesis in polycystic kidney disease in mouse models (Natoli et al., 2010), suggesting a possible conserved link between GlcCer and TOR activities.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observation in mouse models.

claim: It is currently unknown whether an iso-branched LCB is also required for the potential role of GlcCer in mammals.
source: It is currently unknown whether an iso-branched LCB is also required for the potential role of GlcCer in mammals, given that most LCBs in mammals are straight-chain LCBs.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of knowledge in the literature.

claim: mmBCFAs (derived from branched-chain amino acids) are present in mammals.
source: However, it is important to note that mmBCFAs (derived from branched-chain amino acids) are also present in mammals.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: mmBCFAs are constituents of sphingolipids in skin cells and the intestinal tract of human newborns.
source: For example, they are constituents of sphingolipids in skin cells and the intestinal tract of human newborns.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: mmBCFAs are found to be incorporated into LCBs (to form an iso- or an anteiso-LCB similar to that in C. elegans) in multiple mammalian tissues.
source: They are also found to be incorporated into LCBs (to form an iso- or an anteiso-LCB similar to that in C. elegans) in multiple mammalian tissues (Aungst, 1989; Karlsson, 1997; Oku et al., 2000; Ran-Ressler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mmBCFAs may have important physiological functions in mammals, including possible roles in ceramide-involved growth regulation.
source: Therefore, their important physiological functions, including possible roles in ceramide-involved growth regulation, may be assumed, albeit not yet uncovered experimentally.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the presence of mmBCFAs in mammals.

claim: Recent work in mammalian cells has indicated that TORC1, for its role in sensing amino acids, localizes at the surface of the lysosome, likely in lipid rafts.
source: Recent work in mammalian cells has indicated that TORC1, for its role in sensing amino acids, localizes at the surface of the lysosome, likely in lipid rafts (Nada et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: d17iso-GlcCer could act as a ligand that binds to a 'receptor' to either repress the NPRL-2/3 complex or activate the TOR complex at the surface of the lysosome.
source: If such a mechanism is conserved in all animals, conceptually, d17iso-GlcCer could act as a ligand that binds to a 'receptor' to either repress the NPRL-2/3 complex or activate the TOR complex at the surface of the lysosome.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the mechanism of action of d17iso-GlcCer.

claim: d17iso-GlcCer could be required for lysosome biogenesis or could be an essential constituent of the membrane microdomain that permits the proper localization or activity of TORC1 on the lysosome.
source: Alternatively, this lipid could be required for lysosome biogenesis or could be an essential constituent of the membrane microdomain that permits the proper localization or activity of TORC1 on the lysosome.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the mechanism of action of d17iso-GlcCer.

claim: No obvious defects in lysosome formation were observed in elo-5(−) mutants.
source: By examining lysosomal markers LMP-1::GFP (Artal-Sanz et al., 2006; O'Rourke et al., 2009; Rabbitts et al., 2008), GLO-1::GFP (Schroeder et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010), and Neutral red (Long et al., 2002), we did not observe obvious defects in lysosome formation in elo-5(−) mutants (Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Major defects in lysosome formation would be inconsistent with the genetic suppression data and previous studies on GlcCer by others.
source: Major defects in lysosome formation would also be inconsistent with our genetic suppression data and previous studies on GlcCer by others (Entchev et al., 2008; van der Poel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the genetic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: One possible mechanism is that d17iso-GlcCer acts through the V-ATPase pathway.
source: One possible mechanism is that d17iso-GlcCer acts through the V-ATPase pathway, since the lysosomal V-ATPase has been shown to be stimulated by GlcCer and to play an essential role in TORC1 activation in studies using tissue culture cells (van der Poel et al., 2011; Zoncu et al., 2011; Bar-Peled et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on previous studies in tissue culture cells.

claim: The lysosomal V-ATPase has been shown to be stimulated by GlcCer and to play an essential role in TORC1 activation in studies using tissue culture cells.
source: One possible mechanism is that d17iso-GlcCer acts through the V-ATPase pathway, since the lysosomal V-ATPase has been shown to be stimulated by GlcCer and to play an essential role in TORC1 activation in studies using tissue culture cells (van der Poel et al., 2011; Zoncu et al., 2011; Bar-Peled et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of TORC1 bypasses the robust L1 arrest phenotype caused by either mmBCFA or d17iso-GlcCer deficiency.
source: It may be important to point out again that activation of TORC1 bypasses the robust L1 arrest phenotype caused by either mmBCFA or d17iso-GlcCer deficiency.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the key findings of the study.

claim: The elo-5(−); nprl-3(ku540) double mutants, still deficient for mmBCFAs and d17iso-GlcCer, propagate continuously.
source: Remarkably, the elo-5(−); nprl-3(ku540) double mutants, still deficient for these lipids, propagate continuously.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The only essential biochemical role of d17iso-GlcCer might be to activate TORC1 or repress NPRL-3.
source: Therefore, the only essential biochemical role of d17iso-GlcCer might be to activate TORC1 or repress NPRL-3.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that bypassing the lipid requirement is achieved by modifying TORC1 or NPRL-3.

claim: The biochemical mechanism underlying the role of d17iso-GlcCer appears to be very specifically connected to TORC1 activation.
source: In other words, the biochemical mechanism underlying this role of d17iso-GlcCer appears to be very specifically connected to TORC1 activation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical data.
